title: The Easter Night and the Cross as Lampstand
english: The heavens shine bright with the dancing of the stars, and all things gleam brighter still as the dawn-bringer rises. Yet this present night is not so much lit up by stars as it exults because our God and Savior has conquered. "Take courage," he says, "for I have conquered the world" (John 16:33). Since God has defeated the invisible enemy, we too shall rightly carry off the victory over demons. Let us stay by the saving cross, so that we may carry off the first-fruits of Jesus' gifts. Let us celebrate this holy night with holy torches, raising an inspired song and singing a heavenly hymn. The Sun of Righteousness, our Lord Jesus Christ, has illumined this present day for the whole circle of the inhabited world; he rose through the cross and rescued the faithful.

No one, then, should disbelieve the signs of the cross. Rather, let everyone worship the blessed and thrice-blessed wood of the cross, and the signs of the cross of him who opened the doors of heaven for us. They no longer "light a lamp and put it under a bushel" — by the bushel I mean the Law — "but on the lampstand," and by the lamp I mean the Word (Matthew 5:15). The Word happened to be under the Law and was hidden from unbelievers, just as a lamp is hidden under a bushel. But when he came upon the cross and was set upon the lampstand, then to the inhabited world.
translator_notes: The row ends mid-sentence: τότε τῷ τῆς οἰκουμένης continues with κύκλῳ κατέλαμψεν in u01-rem-early.
'The sun of righteousness' is Malachi 4:2, which is LXX Malachi 3:20.
The second dative τοῖς τοῦ σταυροῦ συμβόλοις is taken as an object of προσκυνείτω.
baehrens: PG 93; Homilia i in sanctum pascha (Khazarzar) u01 open
orientation: Hesychius of Jerusalem opens his Easter homily by contrasting the natural brightness of the heavens with the surpassing joy of this night because Christ has conquered the world and the invisible enemy; he urges the congregation to cling to the saving cross and worship the wood of the cross as the lampstand on which the Word now shines to the whole world.
